Let \(N=2004\). Since \(f(1)=2004\), no element of \(S\) is \(1\); hence no \(a_i\) is coprime to itself.

Let \(G\) be the graph on \(S\) where two distinct elements are adjacent iff they are not coprime. If the common value is \(m<2003\), then each vertex has degree
\[
d=2003-m\ge 1.
\]
So \(G\) is a positive-degree regular graph.

A pairwise coprime subset of \(S\) is an independent set in \(G\). If an independent set has size \(r\), then all \(d\) neighbors of each of its vertices lie outside it, giving \(rd\) edges from it to the outside. The outside vertices have total degree \((2004-r)d\), so
\[
rd\le (2004-r)d.
\]
Since \(d>0\), this gives \(r\le 1002\). Thus every subset of size \(1003\) contains two non-coprime elements.

This bound is sharp: choose distinct primes \(p_{ij}\) for \(1\le i,j\le 1002\), and set
\[
a_i=\prod_{j=1}^{1002}p_{ij},\qquad b_j=\prod_{i=1}^{1002}p_{ij}.
\]
Then the \(a_i\)'s are pairwise coprime, the \(b_j\)'s are pairwise coprime, but every \(a_i,b_j\) share \(p_{ij}\). Hence every element is coprime to exactly \(1001\) others, and there is a pairwise coprime \(1002\)-subset.

Therefore the least \(k\) is
\[
\boxed{1003}.
\]
